ox: Correct. MZ (identical) twins share nearly all genes. If they are more alike than DZ twins, even when raised apart, genes likely play a role in the trait.
Twins raised apart do not share a family environment, so it cannot be the sole cause of their similarity.
MZ concordance is rarely 100 percent, so environment still matters. The study shows genes contribute, not that they decide everything.
Random error would not make genetically identical twins systematically more alike.

p: Monozygotic (MZ) twins come from one egg and share nearly 100 percent of their genes. Dizygotic (DZ) twins share about 50 percent. Concordance is how often both twins have the trait.
If MZ twins match more than DZ twins, genes likely contribute to the trait.

mem: MZ about 100 percent genes; DZ about 50 percent.
Higher MZ than DZ concordance means genetic influence.
Heritability is not complete determination.
d_7A_1.trap: Treating high heritability as meaning genes alone decide the trait.
d_7A_1.plain: If two copies of a recipe give very similar cakes in different kitchens, the recipe matters a lot.

ox: James-Lange says arousal alone defines the emotion. It cannot explain why the same injection led to anger or euphoria.
Correct. Two-factor theory says emotion equals arousal plus a cognitive label. The confederate's behavior gave the label (angry or happy).
Cannon-Bard says arousal and emotion happen at the same time and does not involve situational labels.
Facial feedback is about facial expressions changing emotion. The study used injections and social cues.

p: Two-factor theory says emotion needs two things: physical arousal and a mental label for it. The label comes from the situation.
In the study, the same epinephrine caused anger or euphoria depending on how the confederate acted.

mem: Emotion equals arousal plus cognitive label.
Schachter-Singer epinephrine study.
James-Lange: arousal first, then emotion.
Cannon-Bard: both at the same time.
d_7A_14.trap: Ignoring the confederate. The situation supplying the label is the key.
d_7A_14.plain: Your heart pounds. At a roller coaster you call it excitement. In a dark alley you call it fear.

ox: Correct. Dissociative identity disorder (DID) means two or more distinct identities or states, with memory gaps beyond normal forgetting.
Borderline personality disorder involves unstable mood, relationships, and self-image. It does not involve separate identities.
Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder with hallucinations and delusions. It is not split identity, despite the name.
Schizoid personality disorder means detachment and little emotion in relationships. It does not involve identity states.

p: Dissociative disorders involve a break in memory, awareness, or identity. In DID, a person has two or more distinct identities.
Memory gaps are more than normal forgetting. Often they involve everyday events.

mem: DID: multiple identities plus amnesia.
Schizophrenia is not split personality.
Dissociative amnesia and fugue are related disorders.
d_7A_25.trap: Equating schizophrenia with split personality. Schizophrenia is about psychosis.
d_7A_25.plain: Like one phone that gets used by two people, each with a different profile who cannot see the other's messages.

ox: Low acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction causes muscle weakness (as in myasthenia gravis), not hallucinations.
Losing GABA inhibition in the spinal cord leads to spasms or tetanus-like effects, not psychosis.
Correct. The dopamine hypothesis links positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions) to too much dopamine in mesolimbic pathways. Antipsychotics block D2 receptors.
Low serotonin is linked to depression. It is not the dopamine hypothesis, and the word only is also a warning sign.

p: Positive symptoms are things added to normal behavior, like hallucinations and delusions. The hypothesis says they come from too much dopamine activity in the mesolimbic pathway.
Antipsychotic drugs block D2 dopamine receptors, which supports this idea.

mem: Positive symptoms: excess dopamine, mesolimbic.
Antipsychotics block D2 receptors.
Parkinson's: too little dopamine.
d_7A_3.trap: Mixing up Parkinson's (too little dopamine) with schizophrenia (too much).
d_7A_3.plain: Too much volume on a radio. The brain hears signals too loudly, so it picks up things that are not there.

ox: Correct. Antisocial personality disorder is a long-term pattern of lying, breaking others' rights, and lacking remorse.
Avoidant personality disorder means shyness and fear of rejection. It is the opposite of ignoring others' rights.
Dependent personality disorder means needing others to take care of you and being submissive.
Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder means perfectionism and rigid control, not harming others without guilt.

p: Personality disorders are lasting patterns of behavior that cause problems in life. They are grouped into clusters.
Antisocial personality disorder is in Cluster B, the dramatic or impulsive group. It involves deceit, rule-breaking, and no remorse.

mem: Antisocial: deceit, rights violations, no remorse.
Cluster B: antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic.
Avoidant and dependent are Cluster C (anxious).
d_7A_37.trap: Choosing avoidant or dependent just because all are personality disorders.
d_7A_37.plain: A kid who breaks the rules, lies, and shrugs when someone gets hurt.

ox: Correct. Displacement redirects an impulse (anger at the boss) toward a safer target (the dog).
Projection means putting your own unwanted feelings onto someone else, such as 'you are angry at me'.
Reaction formation means acting the opposite of how you feel, such as being extra nice to someone you dislike.
Sublimation means turning an impulse into something socially acceptable, like using anger for sports.

p: Defense mechanisms are unconscious ways the mind handles uncomfortable feelings. Displacement moves a feeling from the real source to a safer target.
The boss is risky to yell at, so the dog gets it.

mem: Displacement: safer target.
Projection: blame feelings on others.
Reaction formation: do the opposite.
Sublimation: channel into good outlets.
q102.trap: Confusing displacement (same feeling, new target) with sublimation (same feeling, healthy outlet).
q102.plain: You are mad at your sister but you slam your door and yell at your teddy bear.

ox: Correct. Yerkes-Dodson is an inverted U. Performance peaks at a moderate arousal level, and the peak sits lower for hard (complex) tasks.
Wrong. Very high arousal (panic, extreme stress) makes performance drop. The trap is thinking more energy always means better results.
Wrong. Very low arousal means boredom and poor focus, so performance is low. The trap is thinking calm is always best.
Wrong. The whole law says arousal does change performance, in an inverted-U shape.

p: Arousal means how alert and activated your body and brain are. The Yerkes-Dodson law says performance is best at a moderate level of arousal. Too little and you are bored. Too much and you are overwhelmed.
The best level depends on the task. Hard tasks do best with lower arousal. Easy or well-practiced tasks do best with higher arousal.

mem: Performance vs arousal is an inverted U
Moderate arousal is best
Complex tasks peak at lower arousal; simple tasks peak at higher arousal
q103.trap: Choosing 'as high as possible' because motivation sounds good. The law is about a middle sweet spot.
q103.plain: Think of a guitar string: too loose and it makes no sound, too tight and it snaps, just right sounds good.

ox: Correct. The smoker holds two conflicting ideas: smoking is harmful, and I smoke. Dismissing the studies changes the belief to match the behavior, which lowers the discomfort. That is cognitive dissonance reduction.
Wrong. Fundamental attribution error is blaming other people's behavior on their personality and ignoring the situation. This is about the smoker's own conflict, not judging others.

Wrong. Confirmation bias is favoring information that agrees with what you already believe. It may play a part, but the key feature here is easing the clash between belief and behavior. The word 'only' is the trap.
Wrong. Self-efficacy is your belief in your own ability to succeed at a task. Nothing here is about ability.

p: Cognitive dissonance is the unpleasant tension you feel when your beliefs and your actions do not match. People want to remove that tension.
They can change the behavior, change the belief, or add a new belief that excuses the behavior. Calling the health studies exaggerated is changing the belief to fit the action.

mem: Dissonance = belief and behavior conflict, causing discomfort
Ways to reduce: change behavior, change belief, add excuse
Fundamental attribution error is about judging OTHERS
Self-efficacy = belief in your own ability
q104.trap: Picking confirmation bias. Look for the clash between what someone knows and what they do.
q104.plain: You eat a whole cake while on a diet and say 'it was a small cake anyway.' You changed the story to feel better.

ox: Correct. 'I didn't study enough' puts the cause inside the person (own effort), which is an internal locus of control.
Wrong. Luck is outside your control, so this is an external locus. The trap is that it sounds like a personal statement because it says 'I'.
Wrong. Blaming the professor puts the cause on another person, so it is external.
Wrong. Test difficulty is a feature of the situation, so it is external.

p: Locus of control is where you believe the causes of outcomes lie. Internal means you think your own actions and effort cause results. External means you think luck, other people, or the situation cause them.
Ask one question: is the cause inside me or outside me?

mem: Internal = my effort, my choices
External = luck, fate, other people, situation
Internal locus is linked with more persistence and better coping
q105.trap: Every option starts with 'I failed because', but only the one naming your own action is internal.
q105.plain: If you lose a game and say 'I should have practiced,' that is internal. If you say 'the referee cheated,' that is external.

ox: Correct. Identical twins share nearly all their genes. If they are alike even in different homes, genes likely play a big role in the trait.
Wrong. If the environment alone made the trait, twins in different homes should differ. They are similar, so this does not fit.
Wrong. One finding cannot show genes are the only cause. Heritability is almost never 100 percent, and environment still matters. 'Entirely' and 'fully' are the traps.
Wrong. The twins were raised apart, so they did not share a family environment.

p: Identical (monozygotic) twins come from one egg and share almost all their genes. Studying them when raised apart separates genes from shared family environment.
High similarity in different environments points to genetic influence. It does not prove genes are the only influence.

mem: Identical twins share about 100% of genes; fraternal about 50%
Twins raised apart test genes vs environment
Similar when apart means substantial genetic contribution, not total
q106.trap: Absolute words like 'entirely' or 'fully determined' are almost always wrong in behavior genetics.
q106.plain: Two copies of the same recipe baked in different kitchens come out tasting alike, so the recipe matters a lot.

ox: Correct. Dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area send signals to the nucleus accumbens (the reward pathway). Addictive drugs raise dopamine there, which makes the behavior feel worth repeating.
Wrong. Acetylcholine drives muscles and is involved in attention and memory. It is not the main reward signal.
Wrong. Glycine is an inhibitory transmitter mostly in the spinal cord and brainstem, not the reward pathway.
Wrong. GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter. Many drugs act on GABA, which makes it tempting, but it is not the reward signal itself.

p: The reward pathway (mesolimbic pathway) runs from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) in the midbrain to the nucleus accumbens. Dopamine is the chemical messenger released along it.
Food, sex, and addictive drugs all raise dopamine here. This teaches the brain to repeat the behavior.

mem: Reward pathway: VTA to nucleus accumbens
Neurotransmitter: dopamine
Addictive drugs boost dopamine in this pathway
GABA and glycine are inhibitory
x7A_001.trap: Choosing GABA because alcohol and sedatives act on it. Reward and reinforcement mean dopamine.
x7A_001.plain: Dopamine is the brain's 'good job, do that again' sticker.

ox: Correct. The nigrostriatal pathway carries dopamine from the substantia nigra to the striatum and controls smooth movement. Blocking D2 receptors there causes tremor and rigidity, like Parkinson disease.
Wrong. The tuberoinfundibular pathway controls prolactin release. Blocking it raises prolactin, not tremor.
Wrong. The mesocortical pathway goes to the prefrontal cortex and affects thinking and motivation, not movement.
Wrong. The mesolimbic pathway is the reward pathway. Blocking it is the intended antipsychotic effect, not the cause of motor side effects.

p: Dopamine travels in several pathways. The nigrostriatal pathway (substantia nigra to striatum) controls movement. Losing dopamine here causes Parkinson disease.
An antipsychotic that blocks D2 receptors hits all pathways. The side effect you see tells you which pathway is involved. Movement problems point to nigrostriatal.

mem: Nigrostriatal = movement (Parkinson)
Mesolimbic = reward, positive psychosis symptoms
Mesocortical = cognition, motivation
Tuberoinfundibular = prolactin
x7A_002.trap: Picking mesolimbic because antipsychotics target it. The question asks about the side effect, which is movement.
x7A_002.plain: A drug that cuts one phone line in a town also cuts the line to the movement office, so movement gets jerky.

ox: Wrong. The parietal lobe handles touch and spatial awareness. Damage causes problems like neglect, not impulsivity.
Wrong. The medulla controls breathing and heart rate. A rod injury there would likely be fatal, not just change personality.
Correct. The prefrontal cortex, at the front of the brain, handles planning, impulse control, and social judgment. This is the Phineas Gage case.
Wrong. The temporal lobe handles hearing, language comprehension, and memory, not social conduct.

p: The prefrontal cortex sits at the very front of the brain. It is the brain's executive center: it plans, makes decisions, and holds back inappropriate urges.
Phineas Gage survived an iron rod through his frontal lobe. His memory and intelligence stayed mostly fine, but he became impulsive and rude.

mem: Prefrontal cortex = planning, impulse control, social judgment
Phineas Gage = frontal damage, personality change
Parietal = touch and space; temporal = hearing, memory, language
x7A_007.trap: Choosing the temporal lobe because it is near the injury area. Social and impulse changes mean frontal.
x7A_007.plain: The prefrontal cortex is the brakes on a car. Without them, you still go, but you cannot stop yourself.

ox: Wrong. The eyes and visual cortex still work. The image reaches the right hemisphere's visual cortex even with the corpus callosum cut.
Correct. The left visual field goes to the right hemisphere. That side usually lacks speech, so they cannot name the key, but it controls the left hand, which can pick the key.
Wrong. The right hand is controlled by the left hemisphere, which never saw the key. Naming also needs the left hemisphere.
Wrong. Naming needs the left hemisphere (speech), which did not receive the image. The right hemisphere can still guide the left hand.

p: The corpus callosum is the bundle of fibers that lets the two brain halves share information. In split-brain patients it is cut.
Each visual field goes to the opposite hemisphere: left field to right hemisphere. In most people, speech is in the left hemisphere. The right hemisphere controls the left hand.

mem: Left visual field goes to right hemisphere
Language is usually in the left hemisphere
Each hemisphere controls the opposite hand
Split brain = corpus callosum cut
x7A_010.trap: Mixing up sides. Trace the path: left field, right brain, left hand, no speech.
x7A_010.plain: Two offices in a building with the hallway between them blocked. One office saw the memo but cannot talk, so it can only point.

ox: Wrong. Winning raises testosterone, so behavior does change hormone levels.
Wrong. The findings show a two-way link, not a single cause. Calling it the sole cause is an overreach.
Correct. Testosterone promotes dominance, and winning raises testosterone. Each affects the other.
Wrong. Testosterone influences behavior in all sexes. Nothing here limits it to males.

p: Hormones can change behavior, and behavior can change hormones. This is called a bidirectional (two-way) relationship.
Here, higher testosterone goes with dominance, and winning raises testosterone further. A feedback loop like this means you cannot say one thing is the only cause.

mem: Hormones and behavior influence each other both ways
Correlation does not show a single cause
Winning tends to raise testosterone
x7A_016.trap: Picking 'sole cause.' Words like 'sole' and 'only' are red flags on the MCAT.
x7A_016.plain: It is like a thermostat and a room: the thermostat changes the heat, and the heat changes what the thermostat does.

ox: Wrong. Heritability describes a whole population, not one person. You cannot say 60 percent of your own trait is genetic.
Correct. Heritability is the share of differences between people in a population that is linked to genetic differences.
Wrong. Heritability is not the chance of passing a trait to a child. It is about variation in a group.
Wrong. Even highly heritable traits can change with environment. Heritability does not mean fixed.

p: Heritability is a number from 0 to 1. It tells you how much of the differences between people in one group, at one time, is linked to differences in their genes.
It does not tell you about one person, it does not predict inheritance odds, and it does not mean a trait cannot change.

mem: Heritability applies to populations, not individuals
It is about variation (differences)
It can change if the environment changes
High heritability does not mean unchangeable
x7A_019.trap: Reading 0.6 as 'my trait is 60 percent genes.' It is about group differences.
x7A_019.plain: If a class's test score differences are 60 percent due to study time, that tells you about the class, not about how much any one kid's score came from studying.

ox: Wrong. MZ (identical) twins come from one fertilized egg that splits. DZ (fraternal) twins come from two eggs.
Correct. If MZ twins are treated more alike than DZ twins, their extra similarity is partly environmental, but the method credits it to genes. That inflates heritability.
Wrong. Twins raised together do share a family environment. That is the point of the design.
Wrong. DZ twins share about 50 percent of their varying genes, like ordinary siblings, not 100 percent.

p: Twin studies compare how alike identical (MZ) and fraternal (DZ) twins are. MZ share about 100 percent of genes and DZ about 50 percent. More similarity in MZ is credited to genes.
This assumes both kinds of twins have equally similar environments. If MZ twins are dressed alike and spend more time together, genes get too much credit.

mem: MZ = one egg, about 100% shared genes
DZ = two eggs, about 50% shared genes
Equal environments assumption can be violated, inflating heritability
x7A_021.trap: Choosing a genetics fact that sounds wrong-ish. The flaw is about environment, not DNA.
x7A_021.plain: If the twins who look identical are also treated like copies, you cannot tell if their sameness comes from their looks or how people act toward them.

ox: Wrong. Evocative correlation is when a child's traits cause others to react a certain way, such as a cheerful baby getting more smiles. Here the child is choosing situations.
Wrong. Epigenetics means chemical changes that turn genes on or off without changing DNA. It is not about choosing settings.
Wrong. Passive correlation is when parents give both the genes and the home environment. Here the child is acting on their own.
Correct. Active correlation (niche-picking) means people choose environments that fit their inherited tendencies.

p: Gene-environment correlation means genes help shape the environments a person experiences. There are three types.
Passive: parents provide both genes and environment. Evocative: your traits make others respond to you. Active: you pick settings that fit your traits.

mem: Passive = parents supply genes and environment
Evocative = traits draw reactions from others
Active = you choose your niche
Epigenetics = gene expression changes, not DNA sequence
x7A_023.trap: Confusing active with evocative. Ask: who is doing the choosing, the person or others?
x7A_023.plain: A kid who loves music joins the band, then gets even better at music.

ox: Wrong. Parkinson disease causes resting tremor and slowed movement from loss of dopamine neurons. It is not caused by a CAG repeat.
Wrong. Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease that destroys myelin. It is not a repeat expansion.
Wrong. Alzheimer disease mainly causes memory loss and does not cause jerky movements or CAG repeats.
Correct. Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant CAG repeat disorder. It causes chorea (jerky movements), mood changes, and dementia as the striatum degenerates.

p: Huntington disease is a genetic disorder caused by too many CAG repeats in one gene. It is autosomal dominant, so one copy of the gene is enough to cause it.
Neurons in the striatum (part of the basal ganglia) die. This causes chorea (involuntary jerky movements), mood and personality changes, and cognitive decline.

mem: Huntington = CAG repeat, autosomal dominant
Symptoms: chorea, mood changes, dementia
Parkinson = slow movement and resting tremor, loss of dopamine neurons
x7A_028.trap: Choosing Parkinson because both are movement disorders. The CAG repeat and jerky movements mean Huntington.
x7A_028.plain: A word gets copy-pasted too many times in a recipe until the recipe stops working.

ox: Wrong. Neurogenesis (making new neurons) does not clear amyloid plaques. The pathology was the same at autopsy.
Wrong. Retrograde amnesia is losing memories from before an injury. It is not about being resilient to damage.
Correct. Cognitive reserve means education and mental activity build richer neural networks that tolerate damage, so symptoms show later.
Wrong. Diagnostic overshadowing means blaming new symptoms on an existing diagnosis. It does not explain fewer symptoms.

p: Cognitive reserve is the brain's ability to cope with damage. Education, mentally active jobs, and learning build richer networks of connections.
With more reserve, the brain can find other routes around damage. Two people can have the same disease changes but very different symptoms.

mem: Cognitive reserve = resilience from education and mental activity
Same pathology, fewer symptoms
It works by compensation, not by removing plaques
x7A_031.trap: Picking neurogenesis because it sounds like repair. The brain compensates; it does not remove the plaques.
x7A_031.plain: A city with many roads can handle a closed road. A town with one road gets stuck.

ox: Correct. Walter Mischel argued that traits predict behavior across different situations only weakly. This started the person-situation debate.
Wrong. Raymond Cattell built a trait model (16 personality factors). He supported traits rather than criticizing them.
Wrong. Hans Eysenck defended trait dimensions and tied them to biology.
Wrong. Abraham Maslow was a humanistic theorist known for the hierarchy of needs, not a critic of traits.

p: Trait theories say stable personality traits explain behavior. Walter Mischel pointed out that people act quite differently in different situations, so traits predict single behaviors poorly.
The modern view is interactionist: traits predict behavior averaged over many situations, and situations matter too.

mem: Mischel = critic of traits, situationism
Cattell = 16 factors; Eysenck = biological trait dimensions
Maslow = humanistic, hierarchy of needs
Modern view = interactionist
x7A_046.trap: Picking a famous trait theorist. The critic is the one who stresses the situation.
x7A_046.plain: A kid can be loud at recess and quiet in class. Calling them just 'loud' misses the situation.

ox: Wrong. Eysenck's theory centered on the reticular activating system, not the size of the amygdala.
Wrong. Eysenck did not blame introversion on excess dopamine in the striatum.
Correct. Introverts already have higher baseline cortical arousal, so a loud party pushes them past a comfortable level and they avoid it.
Wrong. Low baseline arousal is Eysenck's explanation for extraverts, who seek stimulation to reach a comfortable level. This is the reversal trap.

p: Eysenck linked extraversion and introversion to baseline cortical arousal, controlled by the reticular activating system. Baseline arousal is how alert the brain is at rest.
Introverts start high, so they avoid extra stimulation. Extraverts start low, so they seek it out.

mem: Introvert = high baseline arousal, avoids stimulation
Extravert = low baseline arousal, seeks stimulation
Based on the reticular activating system
x7A_048.trap: Reversing the two types. Remember: introverts are already full, so they avoid more.
x7A_048.plain: If your cup is already almost full, you do not want more water poured in. If it is empty, you want a lot.

ox: Wrong. Social cognitive researchers measure beliefs such as self-efficacy (confidence in your own ability) and expectancies, usually by questionnaire. The trap is picking it because the test is about 'thinking'.

Correct. Projective tests (Thematic Apperception Test, Rorschach) give vague pictures or inkblots. The idea is that people read their hidden, unconscious motives into the vague image. That idea comes from Freud's psychoanalytic tradition.
Wrong. Trait researchers use structured self-report questionnaires with fixed items, such as the NEO-PI. The trap is that both are 'personality tests', but trait tests are not open-ended.
Wrong. Behaviorists study observable behavior and its consequences, not hidden motives. Telling a story about a picture is not what they measure.

concept.t: Projective tests and the psychoanalytic view
p: A projective test shows a vague image and asks the person to interpret it. 'Projecting' means putting your own inner feelings onto something outside you.
Psychoanalytic theory says much of the mind is unconscious. Vague images give those hidden motives a way to show up in the person's answers.

mem: Projective tests (TAT, Rorschach) = psychoanalytic
Trait = structured self-report (NEO-PI, Big Five)
Social cognitive = self-efficacy, expectancies
x7A_054.trap: Vague stimulus plus open-ended answer means unconscious motives, so pick psychoanalytic. Fixed questionnaire items means trait.
x7A_054.plain: Like seeing shapes in clouds: what you see says something about what is on your mind.

ox: Wrong. In schizophrenia gray matter (the tissue holding nerve cell bodies) tends to be reduced, especially in temporal and frontal regions. The trap is getting the direction backward.

Correct. Ventricles are fluid-filled spaces in the brain. When surrounding brain tissue shrinks, the ventricles look bigger. Enlarged lateral and third ventricles are the most replicated structural finding.
Wrong. The corpus callosum (the bundle joining the two hemispheres) is not typically absent in schizophrenia. Absence is a rare developmental condition.
Wrong. Schizophrenia is linked to reduced frontal activity (hypofrontality), not enlarged frontal lobes. Again the direction is backward.

p: Schizophrenia shows loss of brain tissue. Gray matter is lower, so the fluid-filled ventricles grow to fill the space.
Frontal lobe activity is also lower, called hypofrontality. This fits poor planning and flat emotion (negative symptoms).

mem: Enlarged ventricles = most consistent finding
Reduced gray matter and hypofrontality
Positive symptoms link to excess dopamine
x7A_064.trap: Answer choices say 'increased' or 'enlarged' for tissue. In schizophrenia, tissue goes down and ventricles go up.
x7A_064.plain: If a cup of ice shrinks, the space around it fills with water. Less brain tissue leaves bigger fluid spaces.

ox: Wrong. If schizophrenia were entirely genetic, identical twins (same DNA) would both have it nearly 100% of the time. 45% is far lower.
Wrong. Identical (MZ) twins at 45% versus fraternal (DZ) twins at 15% is a threefold gap. That gap shows genes matter.
Correct. MZ share nearly all genes, DZ about half. Higher MZ concordance means genes contribute. Concordance below 100% means non-genetic factors matter too. This is the diathesis-stress idea.
Wrong. Both twin types share a family environment roughly equally, yet their concordance differs. So shared environment cannot be the main explanation.

p: Concordance is the chance that if one twin has a trait, the other does too. Identical twins share about 100% of genes. Fraternal twins share about 50%.
Higher concordance in identical twins points to genes. A rate below 100% points to environment. Diathesis-stress: a genetic vulnerability (diathesis) plus stress triggers the illness.

mem: MZ concordance > DZ concordance = genetic influence
MZ concordance < 100% = environment matters
Diathesis-stress = vulnerability plus stressor
x7A_065.sc: Compare MZ to DZ for genes. Compare MZ to 100% for environment.
x7A_065.trap: Extreme answers ('entirely', 'no role') are usually wrong. Choose the balanced answer when MZ is above DZ but under 100%.
x7A_065.plain: If one twin gets a cold, the other often does too, but not always. Something besides shared genes decides it.

ox: Wrong. Phobias are explained mainly by classical conditioning of fear plus avoidance. Learned helplessness is about giving up, not fear.
Wrong. Schizophrenia involves psychosis (hallucinations, delusions), which learned helplessness does not model.
Wrong. OCD involves obsessions and compulsions that reduce anxiety. The dogs stopped trying, which is passivity, not repetitive rituals.
Correct. Dogs learned that nothing they did stopped the shocks, so they stopped trying even when escape was possible. This passivity and hopelessness is used to model depression.

p: Learned helplessness is when repeated uncontrollable bad events teach an animal that its actions do not matter. It then stops trying, even when escape is possible.
Seligman used this to model depression: feeling hopeless and passive after perceived loss of control.

mem: Seligman = learned helplessness
Inescapable shock then no escape attempts
Model of depression
x7A_074.trap: Do not link it to fear or phobias just because shocks are scary. The key is giving up, not fearing.
x7A_074.plain: If you always fail a class no matter how hard you study, you eventually stop studying even for an easy test.

ox: Wrong. Behavioral models say depression involves too little positive reinforcement, not too much.
Wrong. 'Anger turned inward' is the psychoanalytic (Freud) view, and it is inward, not outward. It is not Beck's model.
Wrong. Excess dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway is the dopamine hypothesis of psychosis. Depression involves serotonin and norepinephrine.
Correct. Beck's cognitive triad is negative views of the self, the world and the future. These thoughts keep depression going.

p: Beck says depressed thinking follows a cognitive triad: 'I am worthless', 'the world is bad', 'the future is hopeless'.
Distortions such as overgeneralization (one failure means all failure) keep the pattern going. Cognitive therapy targets these thoughts.

mem: Cognitive triad = self, world, future
Beck = cognitive therapy
Freud = anger turned inward
x7A_075.mn: Triad: Self, World, Future. Say 'S-W-F': Self, World, Future.
x7A_075.trap: Do not mix up Beck (thoughts) with Freud (anger inward) or the dopamine hypothesis (psychosis).
x7A_075.plain: Wearing gray-tinted glasses: everything about you, the world, and tomorrow looks gloomy.

ox: Wrong. Extinction weakens an existing response when the stimulus is no longer paired with the outcome. It does not create a new fear.

Correct. The dog (neutral stimulus) was paired with the painful bite (unconditioned stimulus, which naturally causes fear). The dog became a conditioned stimulus, and fear of dogs is the conditioned response. Her panic at any dog also shows generalization.
Wrong. Observational learning means learning by watching others. She was bitten herself, so direct conditioning explains it.
Wrong. Latent learning is learning that stays hidden until a reward gives a reason to show it. It does not explain a fear response.

p: In classical conditioning a neutral stimulus is paired with an unconditioned stimulus (one that causes a reflex reaction). The neutral stimulus then triggers a similar reaction by itself.
Here dog plus bite leads to dog alone causing fear. Fear spreading to all dogs is stimulus generalization.

mem: NS + US pairing creates CS
Phobia onset = classical conditioning
Generalization = similar stimuli also trigger the response
x7A_078.trap: Observational learning is tempting for phobias, but when she was bitten directly, pick classical conditioning.
x7A_078.plain: A kid touches a hot stove while a bell rings. Soon the bell alone makes the kid flinch.

ox: Wrong. Spontaneous recovery is when an extinguished response returns after a rest period. Avoidance does not cause that.
Correct. Avoiding the object brings relief. Removing an unpleasant feeling is negative reinforcement, so avoidance increases. Also, without exposure, the fear never has a chance to extinguish.
Wrong. Punishment would reduce a behavior. Avoidance gets stronger, so it is reinforced, not punished.
Wrong. Extinction needs exposure to the feared object without the bad outcome. Avoidance prevents exactly that.

p: Mowrer's two-factor theory: fear is learned by classical conditioning, then kept alive by operant conditioning.
Avoiding the object removes anxiety. Removing something unpleasant is negative reinforcement, which makes the avoidance more likely next time.

mem: Negative reinforcement = remove aversive, behavior increases
Avoidance blocks extinction
Exposure therapy treats phobias
x7A_079.trap: Negative reinforcement is not punishment. Reinforcement raises behavior. Punishment lowers it.
x7A_079.plain: If you skip the dentist because it scares you, the relief feels good, so you skip again, and the fear never fades.

ox: Wrong. Generalized anxiety disorder stays in the anxiety disorders class in DSM-5.
Wrong. PTSD was moved out of anxiety disorders too, but into trauma- and stressor-related disorders, not with OCD.
Correct. DSM-5 created obsessive-compulsive and related disorders, which includes OCD, body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding, trichotillomania (hair pulling) and excoriation (skin picking).
Wrong. Panic disorder remains an anxiety disorder in DSM-5.

p: DSM-5 moved OCD out of anxiety disorders into its own class: obsessive-compulsive and related disorders.
Members: OCD, body dysmorphic disorder (preoccupation with a perceived body flaw), hoarding, trichotillomania, excoriation.

mem: OCD, BDD, hoarding, trichotillomania, excoriation share a class
PTSD = trauma- and stressor-related
GAD and panic remain anxiety disorders
x7A_081.trap: Both OCD and PTSD left the anxiety class, but to different classes. Do not pair them together.
x7A_081.plain: DSM-5 sorted the closet: OCD got its own shelf with similar items, repetitive thoughts and behaviors.

ox: Wrong. Illness anxiety disorder is worry about having a serious illness, with few or no actual symptoms. She has a real loss of function.
Wrong. Factitious disorder means deliberately faking or causing symptoms to gain the sick role. Nothing suggests intent here.
Wrong. Somatic symptom disorder centers on excessive thoughts and worry about symptoms. Here the key feature is sudden loss of function that does not fit neurological disease.
Correct. Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder) is a real motor or sensory symptom, such as paralysis, with normal neurological tests, often after stress, and not faked.

p: Conversion disorder means a real neurological-looking symptom (paralysis, blindness, numbness) that does not match any known disease. It often follows psychological stress.
The person is not faking. Faking on purpose is factitious disorder (for sick role) or malingering (for external gain).

mem: Normal tests plus sudden motor or sensory loss after stress = conversion
Not intentional
Illness anxiety = worry without symptoms
x7A_088.trap: Do not choose somatic symptom disorder just because the symptom is physical. Look for worry (somatic) versus loss of function (conversion).
x7A_088.plain: The body 'turns stress into' a symptom, like a fuse blowing to stop overload, though the wiring is fine.

ox: Correct. Somatic symptom disorder means one or more distressing physical symptoms plus excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviors about them. The pain can be real.
Wrong. The tempting choice. Her worry is anxiety-like, but DSM-5 puts worry focused on bodily symptoms in somatic symptom and related disorders.
Wrong. Dissociative disorders involve disrupted memory, identity or awareness. She has none of these.
Wrong. Neurocognitive disorders involve decline in thinking or memory, such as dementia. She has no such decline.

p: Somatic means 'of the body'. In this disorder a person has bodily symptoms and spends excessive time and energy worrying about them.
The symptoms can be real, such as pain, and need not be medically unexplained. The problem is the disproportionate focus.

mem: Somatic symptom disorder = real symptom + excessive worry
Illness anxiety = worry with few symptoms
Conversion = neurological loss without disease
x7A_090.trap: Excess worry makes anxiety disorders tempting. When the worry is about bodily symptoms, pick somatic symptom.
x7A_090.plain: Like checking a small scratch hundreds of times a day. The scratch is real, but the worry takes over life.

ox: Wrong. Dependent personality disorder means clinging, submissive behavior and a need to be taken care of. It does not include rapid idealizing and devaluing.
Correct. Borderline personality disorder: unstable relationships, self-image and emotions, fear of abandonment, self-harm, and splitting (seeing people as all good or all bad).
Wrong. Histrionic means attention seeking and dramatic emotion, not self-harm and splitting.
Wrong. Bipolar II has hypomanic and depressive episodes lasting days to weeks. Borderline shifts occur within hours and are triggered by relationships.

p: Borderline personality disorder has an unstable sense of self, intense unstable relationships, impulsivity and self-harm.
Splitting means seeing others as all good (idealizing) or all bad (devaluing), switching quickly.

mem: Splitting = idealize then devalue
Fear of abandonment, self-harm
Cluster B personality disorder
x7A_093.trap: Mood swings tempt you toward bipolar. Bipolar episodes last days to weeks. Borderline shifts last hours and track relationships.
x7A_093.plain: A person who sees friends as heroes one day and villains the next, with nothing in between.

ox: Correct. Avoidant personality disorder: wants relationships but fears criticism and rejection, and feels inadequate.
Wrong. Paranoid personality disorder involves distrust and suspicion of others' motives, not a wish for friends.
Wrong. Antisocial personality disorder involves disregard for others' rights, not fear of rejection.
Wrong. Schizoid individuals genuinely do not want close relationships and show limited emotion. This man desperately wants friends.

p: Both avoidant and schizoid people have few relationships, but for different reasons.
Avoidant: wants connection, fears rejection. Schizoid: indifferent to connection.

mem: Avoidant = wants friends, fears rejection (Cluster C)
Schizoid = indifferent (Cluster A)
Paranoid = suspicious (Cluster A)
x7A_095.sc: Ask 'Does he want friends?' Yes means avoidant. No means schizoid.
x7A_095.trap: Both have few friends. The key is whether the person wants friends.
x7A_095.plain: Avoidant is the kid who wants to join the game but is afraid to ask. Schizoid is the kid who would rather play alone.

ox: Wrong. Intrusive, unwanted thoughts the person resists describe OCD obsessions, not OCPD.
Correct. OCPD is a pervasive style of perfectionism, orderliness and control that the person sees as correct (ego-syntonic), without true obsessions. OCD obsessions are unwanted (ego-dystonic).
Wrong. There is no rule that one is always more impairing. Severity varies.
Wrong. OCPD is a personality disorder with no psychosis.

p: OCD has obsessions (unwanted intrusive thoughts) and compulsions (rituals). The person finds them distressing, which is ego-dystonic.
OCPD is a lifelong personality style of perfectionism and control. The person thinks it is right (ego-syntonic) and has no true obsessions.

mem: OCD = ego-dystonic
OCPD = ego-syntonic, no true obsessions
They can co-occur
x7A_096.mn: Syntonic = 'in tune' with self. Dystonic = 'out of tune' with self.
x7A_096.trap: The names are almost the same. Ask whether the person sees the behavior as wrong or unwanted (OCD) or as right (OCPD).
x7A_096.plain: OCD is like a song stuck in your head that you hate. OCPD is like insisting your way of folding towels is simply correct.

ox: Wrong. Anxiety symptoms are usually distressing and unwanted (ego-dystonic).
Wrong. Dissociative identity disorder usually involves distress, memory gaps and confusion.
Correct. Personality disorder traits are typically ego-syntonic: they feel like a natural part of the self, so people feel little distress and may blame others.
Wrong. Depression involves marked personal distress, which is ego-dystonic.

p: Ego-syntonic means the trait feels in harmony with who you are. The person sees it as 'just me' or 'the right way'.
Personality disorders are usually ego-syntonic, so people often do not seek help. Most other disorders are ego-dystonic: unwanted and distressing.

mem: Personality disorders = ego-syntonic
Anxiety, depression, OCD = ego-dystonic
Little distress leads to few people seeking treatment
x7A_098.trap: Low distress about rigid traits points to a personality disorder, not a mood or anxiety disorder.
x7A_098.plain: A kid who thinks being bossy is just being right will not ask for help changing. A kid with a stomachache will.

ox: Wrong. Delirium is a neurocognitive disorder, not a personality disorder.
Wrong. Delirium is often reversible once its cause (medication, infection, metabolic problem) is treated.
Correct. Delirium has acute onset over hours to days, fluctuating attention and an identifiable cause, and is often reversible. Dementia is gradual and progressive.
Wrong. Impaired attention is the core feature of delirium, and the question states that attention fluctuates.

p: Delirium is a sudden disturbance in attention and awareness that fluctuates during the day. Causes include medications, infections and metabolic problems. It often clears when the cause is treated.
Dementia is a slow, progressive decline in memory and thinking, with attention relatively spared early on.

mem: Delirium = acute, fluctuating attention, reversible
Dementia = gradual, progressive
Common in hospitalized older adults
x7A_100.trap: Do not choose 'memory loss only'. Delirium is mainly an attention problem with sudden onset.
x7A_100.plain: Delirium is a sudden storm that can pass. Dementia is slow erosion of a coastline.

ox: Wrong. Spontaneous recovery is the return of an extinguished conditioned response after a rest. Here interest fell below its original level.
Correct. The overjustification effect: an external reward for an activity already enjoyed makes people credit the reward, so intrinsic motivation drops when the reward stops.
Wrong. Learned helplessness comes from uncontrollable aversive events, not from payment.
Wrong. Drive reduction is about satisfying biological needs such as hunger. Drawing is not a biological need.

p: Intrinsic motivation is doing something because you enjoy it. Extrinsic motivation is doing it for rewards.
Paying for an activity you already enjoy can make you think you do it for pay. When pay stops, you stop.

mem: Overjustification = extrinsic reward lowers intrinsic motivation
Applies to activities already enjoyed
Drive reduction = biological need
x7A_110.trap: Do not pick spontaneous recovery. That refers to a conditioned response returning, not motivation dropping.
x7A_110.plain: A kid who loves reading is paid per book. When the pay ends, reading feels like a job, so they stop.

ox: Wrong. This describes incentive theory, where outside rewards pull behavior. The trap is picking the motivation theory you know best instead of the one about emotional rebound.

Correct. A drug causes a first emotional reaction (the high). The brain answers with an opposite reaction (the a-process is followed by the b-process). With repeated use the opposite reaction gets stronger, so the high shrinks (tolerance) and the crash after it feels worse (withdrawal).
Wrong. The theory says the opposing reaction grows with repetition, not that cells die after one use. The trap is the word 'permanently' and the idea of one-time damage.
Wrong. The whole theory is about arousal and emotion shifting, first one way, then the opposite way. Constant arousal would give no tolerance or withdrawal.

p: Opponent-process theory says your body likes to stay balanced. When something causes a strong feeling, such as a drug high, the brain starts an opposite feeling to pull you back to normal.
With repeated use the opposite feeling gets faster and stronger. Tolerance means the same dose gives less of a high. Withdrawal means the opposite feeling shows up when the drug is gone.

mem: Initial reaction is followed by an opposite reaction (Solomon).
Repetition strengthens the opposing process.
Stronger opposite process = tolerance and withdrawal.
Incentive theory = outside rewards, a different idea.
x7A_115.trap: Confusing opponent-process with incentive theory or drive reduction. Look for 'opposite reaction grows with repetition'.
x7A_115.plain: It is like a seesaw. Each time someone pushes one end up, the other end learns to push back harder, so the same push barely lifts it and the drop afterward is bigger.

ox: Correct. Students were assigned a side at random and then argued it out loud. Their attitudes moved toward that side. Acting a role can change what you believe, through self-perception and reducing the discomfort of cognitive dissonance.
Wrong. Because assignment was random, traits cannot explain the change. 'Fully determine' is also too extreme, a common trap word.
Wrong. Drive reduction is about satisfying biological needs like hunger. Debating does not satisfy a bodily need.
Wrong. Here behavior (arguing) came first and the attitude followed. 'Always' is also a red flag word.

p: An attitude is a lasting feeling or opinion about something. People often think attitudes cause behavior. It also works the other way: what you do can change what you think.

Role-playing is one example. When you argue a view, you may start to believe it. Cognitive dissonance is the uncomfortable feeling when actions and beliefs clash, and people reduce it by changing the belief.

mem: Behavior can shape attitudes, not only the reverse.
Role-playing and forced compliance shift attitudes.
Cognitive dissonance: conflict between actions and beliefs, reduced by changing beliefs.
Random assignment rules out prior traits.
x7A_124.trap: Assuming attitudes always come first. Words like 'always' and 'fully' are usually wrong.
x7A_124.plain: If you pretend to be a pirate all day, you may start to feel like one. Acting a part can change how you feel inside.

ox: Correct. The theory of planned behavior says intention depends on attitude toward the act, subjective norms (what important people expect) and perceived behavioral control (how able you feel).
Wrong. Id and superego are Freud's ideas. This model is about conscious intentions. The trap is grabbing a famous psychology term that does not belong.
Wrong. The theory is cognitive and does not rest on conditioning history. 'Only' also makes it too narrow.
Wrong. Heritability is a genetics idea and is not one of the model's factors.

p: This theory predicts what people will do by looking at their intention, or plan, to do it. Intention depends on three things.
Attitude is how you feel about the act. Subjective norms are what people who matter to you expect. Perceived behavioral control is how confident you feel that you can actually do it.

mem: Three inputs: attitude, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control.
They predict intention, and intention predicts behavior.
Subjective norms = what others expect.
It is a cognitive model, not Freudian or genetic.
x7A_125.trap: Picking Freud or genetics terms. The right answer names norms and control.
x7A_125.plain: Will you go to the pool? You like swimming, your friends are going, and you know you can swim. All three make you say yes.

ox: Wrong. The central route means careful thinking about the quality of arguments. Here the person ignored the arguments, so this is not central.
Correct. Attractiveness is a surface cue. Persuasion through cues like looks, credibility or message length is the peripheral route.
Wrong. 'Cognitive route' is not part of the model. The trap is a plausible-sounding made-up name.
Wrong. The model has only two routes, central and peripheral. 'Affective route' is not one of them.

p: This model explains how persuasion works. Elaboration means thinking hard about a message.

If you are motivated and able to think, you take the central route and judge the arguments. If not, you take the peripheral route and are swayed by cues like attractiveness or expertise. Central-route change lasts longer.

mem: Central route = argument quality, lasting change.
Peripheral route = surface cues (looks, credibility, length), weaker change.
Peripheral is used when motivation or ability to think is low.
Only two routes exist.
x7A_128.trap: Inventing routes like 'affective' or 'cognitive'. Only central and peripheral exist.
x7A_128.plain: Choosing a cereal by reading the ingredients is central. Choosing it because the box has a cool cartoon is peripheral.

ox: Wrong. The result shows a mismatch, not that people lie. 'Definitely false' is too strong. People may sincerely believe their stated attitude.
Correct. Slow pairing of the group with positive words hints at a weak automatic positive link. That means implicit (automatic) attitudes may differ from explicit (stated) ones.
Wrong. Attitudes have affective (feeling), behavioral and cognitive parts. The task does not remove the feeling part.
Wrong. Reaction-time tasks like the Implicit Association Test were built to measure implicit attitudes.

p: Explicit attitudes are the ones you know about and can report. Implicit attitudes are automatic links in your mind that you may not notice.
The Implicit Association Test times how fast you pair words and groups. Faster pairing means a stronger link. A gap between the test and self-report shows the two can differ.

mem: Explicit = conscious, self-reported.
Implicit = automatic, measured by reaction time (IAT).
The two can disagree without anyone lying.
Attitudes have affective, behavioral, cognitive parts.
x7A_129.trap: Concluding that a mismatch means dishonesty, or that implicit attitudes cannot be measured.
x7A_129.plain: What you say you like and what your hand grabs first without thinking can be different things.
